1. Start here

Use one organizing chain so the lecture becomes predictable instead of a list of signs.

Clot risk→ DVT forms→ Embolizes to PA→ RV afterload ↑→ RV dilation / strain→ LV preload ↓→ Hypotension / shock
Repeatable exam approach: first ask “Why did a venous clot form?” Then ask “How much pulmonary flow is blocked?” Then “Is the RV coping?” Finally choose “rule-out test, confirmatory imaging, anticoagulation, or reperfusion?”

Professor-emphasis signals

Must know CTPA is the lecture’s initial imaging choice for a stable patient when PE needs to be established.

Must know Anticoagulation is the mainstay for most stable PE; the professor question specifically selects heparin as immediate therapy.

Distinguish PE injures the right heart first. Echo clues include RV dilation, RV:LV >1, and McConnell’s sign.

Trap S1Q3T3, Hampton hump, and Westermark sign are recognition clues; the lecture repeatedly notes that many basic findings are nonspecific.

2. Mechanisms

Reveal one causal link at a time. Turn prediction mode on when you want to force yourself to forecast the next step.

Scenario

Normal bridge: the RV normally ejects into a low-pressure pulmonary circuit. Acute obstruction is dangerous because the RV suddenly faces a load it was not built to handle.

3. PE guide

Lecture-required content organized by the decisions an exam question asks you to make.

Virchow’s triad

ComponentLecture examples
Venous stasisImmobilization, long air/road travel, post-op bedbound state
Endothelial injurySurgery, trauma, especially lower-extremity injury
HypercoagulabilityPregnancy, estrogen/OCPs, malignancy, inherited thrombophilias, polycythemia, chemotherapy

Hypercoagulable states

Hereditary

Antithrombin deficiency · Protein C deficiency · Protein S deficiency · Factor V Leiden

Acquired

Cancer · Pregnancy/postpartum · OCPs · Polycythemia · Smoking · Chemotherapy

Professor logic: think less about “what causes PE” and more about what allowed the venous thrombus to form. PE is usually the downstream event after a clot forms elsewhere and embolizes.

History that should raise suspicion

Long air/road travel · recent surgery · malignancy · smoking · recent lower-extremity trauma · prior PE.

Transcript nuance: the lecturer repeatedly uses sudden unexplained symptoms after a predisposing event. Prior PE matters because recurrence is more likely.

Symptoms / physical exam

FindingWhy it happens
Sudden dyspnea / tachypneaAcute loss of perfusion and gas-exchange inefficiency
Pleuritic chest painPleural irritation, especially with peripheral infarction
HemoptysisPulmonary infarction can injure tissue and bleed
TachycardiaCompensation for impaired forward output / physiologic stress
Hypotension / syncopeLarge clot burden → RV failure → LV underfilling → low output
Calf/thigh pain or swellingClue to the source DVT
Cough / low-grade fever / diaphoresisSupportive but nonspecific lecture findings

Labs

TestUse in lecture
D-dimerFibrin degradation marker; most useful in lower-risk rule-out pathway.
WBCMay rise with inflammatory stress; nonspecific.
ABGAssesses oxygenation.
TroponinSupports myocardial/RV injury or ischemic stress.
BNPSupports pressure/volume stress from a struggling ventricle.

Wells path taught in lecture

<2→D-dimer
2–6→High-sensitivity D-dimer or CTPA
>6→CTPA; do not rely on D-dimer

Imaging hierarchy

StudyWhat to look for
CTPALecture’s initial imaging choice for stable suspected PE; direct clot, extent, RV dilation.
EchoRV dilation, RV:LV >1, McConnell’s sign; fast bedside severity assessment.
V/Q scanNormal ventilation with reduced/absent perfusion; alternative when CT is contraindicated/unavailable.
Chest X-rayUsually nonspecific; Hampton hump / Westermark are classic but uncommon.
ECGSinus tachycardia, RBBB, T inversions V1–V4, S1Q3T3; strain clues, not definitive.
Trap: a dramatic “classic sign” is not the same as the test that establishes PE. The professor’s own question makes this distinction.

Acute RV failure chain

What the clot does to the heart

PA obstruction → RV afterload ↑ → RV dilation → tricuspid insufficiency / RA and venous congestion → RV ischemia and falling RV output → LV preload ↓ → systemic hypotension → shock.

The transcript frames this as a self-amplifying cycle: a strained RV needs more oxygen while coronary perfusion and systemic pressure deteriorate.

Reverse reasoning: if the stem gives syncope, hypotension, RV dilation, elevated troponin/BNP, or an RV:LV ratio >1, ask whether a large PE is producing clinically important RV strain.

Three treatment buckets

BucketLecture role
AnticoagulationMainstay for most patients. Acute agents include LMWH / unfractionated heparin; oral agents include DOACs and warfarin.
ThrombolysisAlteplase/tPA for severe PE with shock/cardiac arrest when appropriate; actively drives fibrin breakdown.
Thrombectomy / catheter therapySelected intermediate-high or unstable patients with large clot burden; mechanically remove clot or deliver local thrombolytic.

Drug anchors

LMWH / UFH: acute anticoagulation options discussed in the lecture.

Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban: factor Xa-directed oral anticoagulants in the slide figure.

Dabigatran: direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor.

Warfarin: older oral option; requires INR monitoring.

Alteplase: plasminogen → plasmin → fibrin degradation.

Course vs clinical-update note: the lecture’s exam framework emphasizes heparin in the acute phase followed by oral therapy. The 2026 AHA/ACC acute-PE guidance says that when initial parenteral therapy is needed, LMWH is preferred over UFH, and eligible patients should generally receive a DOAC rather than a vitamin K antagonist. Use the lecture wording for course-specific questions while recognizing this current clinical nuance.

Put easily confused choices side by side using the same discriminator every time.

vs

Master comparison table

PairShared featureBest discriminatorMechanismTempting trap

5. Recognition lab

Translate patterns into physiology before naming the diagnosis.

ECG

Right-heart strain clues

Sinus tachycardia, RBBB, T-wave inversion V1–V4, and S1Q3T3 can support acute RV strain.

Mechanism: acute RV pressure loading changes right-sided conduction/repolarization. These findings are supportive, not definitive.
Echo

RV response

Look for RV dilation, RV:LV >1, and McConnell’s sign.

Mechanism: sudden pulmonary obstruction raises RV afterload, so the RV dilates while the LV may look relatively underfilled/compressed.
V/Q

Perfusion defect

Ventilation preserved, perfusion reduced.

Mechanism: the airway is open, but a vascular obstruction prevents blood from reaching that ventilated region.

6. Lecture figures

Try to interpret the evidence first. Slide identity and explanation remain hidden until you reveal them.

Figure challenge A

Question: The image contains classic PE-associated radiographic clues. What two named signs should you be able to distinguish, and what does each imply?

Hampton hump: peripheral wedge-shaped opacity → pulmonary infarction. Westermark sign: focal increased translucency → decreased regional perfusion.

Source revealed: lecture slide 12.

Figure challenge B

Question: Which right-heart strain pattern is the lecture asking you to recognize, and how do you decode its name?

S1Q3T3: prominent/deep S in lead I, Q wave in lead III, and inverted T in lead III. Other lecture clues include sinus tachycardia, RBBB, and T inversion V1–V4.

Source revealed: lecture slide 13.

Figure challenge C

Question: Which chamber is abnormally enlarged, and what acute loading condition explains it?

The right ventricle is dilated because pulmonary arterial obstruction acutely raises RV afterload. In the lecture, RV:LV >1 supports RV dilation/strain.

Source revealed: lecture slide 15.

Figure challenge D

Question: If most of the RV free wall is poorly contractile but the apex is relatively preserved, what sign is being described?

McConnell’s sign. The transcript describes a dilated, struggling RV with relative preservation of apical motion.

Source revealed: lecture slide 15.

Figure challenge E

Question: Without memorizing every segment, what is the management logic as patients move from stable categories toward cardiopulmonary failure?

The lecture’s simplification is: stable A–C patients generally receive anticoagulation; when patients reach D/E physiology with hypotension, shock, or cardiopulmonary failure, consider advanced reperfusion strategies such as systemic thrombolysis, catheter therapy/mechanical thrombectomy, or surgery.

Source revealed: lecture slide 19 (2026 AHA/ACC clinical-category figure).

Figure challenge F

Question: What conversion is the key step that makes this therapy dissolve fibrin clot?

Plasminogen → plasmin. Plasmin then degrades fibrin/fibrinogen and promotes clot dissolution.

Source revealed: lecture slide 20.

Figure challenge G

Question: What is the therapeutic advantage of putting the catheter directly at the pulmonary clot?

It permits local lower-dose thrombolytic delivery; the lecture also describes ultrasonic energy loosening fibrin and helping drug penetrate the clot.

Source revealed: lecture slide 22.

8. Exam sheet

Part I — Core framework and must-know content

Virchow risk→DVT→PA obstruction→RV afterload ↑→RV dilation/failure→LV preload ↓→Shock
DomainExam-ready rule
DefinitionPE = thromboembolus blocking one or more pulmonary arteries; most commonly originates from a deep venous clot in the legs.
VirchowStasis + endothelial injury + hypercoagulability. Long travel → stasis; surgery/trauma → stasis + injury; pregnancy/estrogen/cancer → hypercoagulable state.
Hereditary thrombophiliaAntithrombin deficiency, protein C deficiency, protein S deficiency, Factor V Leiden.
Acquired risksCancer, pregnancy/postpartum, OCPs, polycythemia, smoking, chemotherapy.
PresentationSudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, cough/wheeze; tachypnea, tachycardia; DVT leg findings. Large PE can cause syncope/hypotension.
RV mechanismPA obstruction → RV afterload ↑ → RV dilation/TR/venous congestion → RV ischemia/output ↓ → LV preload ↓ → hypotension/obstructive shock.
LabsD-dimer = fibrin degradation marker; troponin = myocardial injury/strain; BNP = pressure/volume stress; ABG assesses oxygenation; WBC may rise nonspecifically.
Wells thresholds taught<2: consider D-dimer. 2–6: high-sensitivity D-dimer or CTPA. >6: CTPA; do not rely on D-dimer.
CTPAInitial imaging choice in stable suspected PE; directly shows clot burden and can show RV dilation.
EchoRV dilation, RV:LV >1, McConnell’s sign. Best for rapid RV consequence/severity assessment, not routine stable-patient clot confirmation.
V/QPE = normal ventilation + reduced/absent perfusion; alternative when CT is contraindicated/unavailable.
Main treatmentMost stable PE → anticoagulation. Severe hypotension/shock/arrest → consider reperfusion/advanced therapy.
AlteplasetPA converts plasminogen → plasmin → fibrin degradation → clot dissolution; major concern = bleeding.
Mechanical / catheterMechanical aspiration debulks clot to restore flow. Catheter-directed therapy delivers local lower-dose thrombolytic; lecture describes ultrasound-assisted fibrin loosening.

Part II — Recognition, distinctions, traps, and question-stem decoding

Distinguish Hampton hump = wedge opacity/infarct; Westermark = focal hyperlucency/oligemia.

Distinguish S1Q3T3 = S in I + Q in III + inverted T in III. Also know sinus tachycardia, RBBB, T inversions V1–V4.

Distinguish CTPA = clot; echo = RV response; D-dimer = rule-out marker; V/Q = perfusion mismatch.

Trap A normal/nonspecific chest X-ray does not exclude PE. Classic X-ray and ECG patterns are not required.

Trap Do not equate anticoagulation with fibrinolysis: anticoagulants mainly prevent propagation/new clot; tPA actively breaks down fibrin.

If the stem gives long travel + calf swelling + sudden dyspnea: identify venous stasis/DVT → PE.

If the stem gives syncope/hypotension + RV dilation: identify large clot burden with acute RV failure and reduced LV filling.

If Wells is low: use the lecture’s D-dimer rule-out branch. If high: go to CTPA.

If the question asks “establish the diagnosis” in a stable patient: favor CTPA over echo/D-dimer.

If shock/arrest appears: the management question has moved from routine anticoagulation toward reperfusion.

If recurrent emboli cause cardiac damage: look at the right heart / tricuspid-RV function, matching the professor practice question.

Drug and treatment micro-table

Agent / strategyTarget / actionCourse clue
UFH / LMWHAnticoagulation through antithrombin-mediated factor inhibitionAcute hospital phase discussed; professor immediate-treatment answer = heparin.
Rivaroxaban / apixaban / edoxabanFactor Xa inhibitionOral options in lecture.
DabigatranDirect thrombin (IIa) inhibitionDo not misclassify it as a Xa inhibitor.
WarfarinVitamin K pathwayRequires INR monitoring.
AlteplasePlasminogen → plasminSystemic fibrinolysis in severe/high-risk PE when appropriate.
Aspiration thrombectomyMechanical clot removalSelected large-burden/intermediate-high or unstable cases.
Lecture-vs-guideline nuance: for this course, preserve the professor’s treatment framing and question logic. Current 2026 AHA/ACC guidance is more specific about category-based hospitalization and advanced therapy, prefers LMWH over UFH when initial parenteral anticoagulation is needed, and recommends DOACs over VKAs for eligible patients.

Clarification 1 — DOAC wording: the transcript conversationally groups the oral agents as direct Xa inhibitors, while the slide’s own coagulation diagram correctly separates rivaroxaban/apixaban/edoxaban (Xa) from dabigatran (direct thrombin/IIa). The guide follows the slide diagram.
Clarification 2 — anticoagulation vs clot dissolution: the lecture’s overall treatment framework distinguishes anticoagulants from thrombolytics. The guide therefore treats heparin/DOACs/warfarin as preventing propagation/new clot while alteplase is the therapy that actively drives plasmin-mediated fibrin breakdown.
